article.title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
article.subtitle: Some of the skepticism about James Talarico’s chances amounts to superstition. But I have one lingering concern about our forecast in Texas.

extraction.summary: Model Talk on FLIPR's 59-61 percent forecast for Democrat James Talarico in the 2026 Texas Senate race. Silver argues against gut-based skepticism, since elections are rare events and Texas polls show no state-specific Democratic bias since 1998, and against using the long Democratic losing streak as evidence. He identifies fundraising as his real concern. FLIPR's fancy fundamentals favor Talarico largely because of a 7:1 fundraising edge, and Silver wonders whether nationalized, ActBlue-driven individual giving has become a weaker signal. The piece details the fundraising variable (individual contributions only, in-state weighted, no party, PAC or self-funding), the binary scandal flag, the toss-up definition, and why ideology is not modeled for non-incumbents.

findings.statement: FLIPR's rating buckets are defined mathematically: a race is a 'toss-up' when neither party has more than a 60 percent chance of winning.
findings.rationale: Some readers are more comfortable with buckets than percentages.
findings.evidence_quote: We describe a race as a “toss-up” when neither party has greater than a 60 percent chance of winning.

findings.statement: The standard generic ballot page put Texas's benchmark at R+4.2, but FLIPR uses a likely-voter-adjusted generic ballot that favored Democrats in 2026, bringing the Texas simple-fundamentals benchmark closer to R+3.
findings.evidence_quote: Our generic ballot page pegs Texas at R +4.2, but FLIPR uses a version of the generic ballot that makes a likely-voter adjustment.

findings.statement: Silver describes FLIPR's simple fundamentals, generic ballot plus a state's partisan lean, as essentially what British analysts call a 'uniform swing'.
findings.evidence_quote: Simple fundamentals consist (simply!) of the generic ballot and a state’s partisan lean score, producing basically what our British readers might call a “uniform swing”.

findings.statement: A scandal flag is worth several points of vote margin in FLIPR's fancy fundamentals, but Silver Bulletin considers the effect of a scandal to be roughly half of what it was a decade or two ago given high polarization. Multiple scandals are folded into one binary flag rather than treated cumulatively.
findings.evidence_quote: Basically, we consider the effect of a scandal to be roughly half what it was a decade or two ago

findings.statement: FLIPR uses individual-contribution fundraising from FEC data as a candidate-quality input because money buys ads and staff, proxies a campaign's organizational skill, and proxies voter enthusiasm. It excludes contributions to party organizations, self-funding and Super PAC spending, for practical reasons and because self-funding often signals a lack of organic support.
findings.evidence_quote: self-funding isn’t a good proxy for voter enthusiasm; in fact, candidates often self-fund because they aren’t generating enough organic support

findings.statement: Silver worries fundraising may now be a less reliable indicator than FLIPR assumes, because giving is highly nationalized and algorithmized through platforms like ActBlue, and Democrats have had a persistent individual-contribution edge in the Trump era. He names revisiting fundraising as a plausible FLIPR improvement for 2028/2030, especially if candidates like Talarico underperform.
findings.evidence_quote: part of me wonders whether fundraising is a less reliable indicator than it once was

findings.statement: FLIPR handles around 1,000 candidates per cycle and would need ideology estimates for past cycles to train on, so it does not quantify ideology for non-incumbents. For incumbents it uses objective party-loyalty scores from congressional votes; defectors such as Collins get a fancy-fundamentals bonus.
findings.rationale: Ideology must be objective and available historically to train on.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR handles around 1000 candidates per cycle between House, Senate and gubernatorial elections, and we’d also need to have estimates for past election cycles to train the model.

findings.statement: In the Silver Bulletin polling database since 1998 (polls in the final three weeks), Texas Democrats have been about as likely to outperform their polling averages as to underperform them. Polls have had an average Democratic bias in recent cycles, but no worse in Texas than nationally, unlike Maine.
findings.evidence_quote: they’ve been roughly as likely to outperform their polling averages as to underperform them.

findings.statement: Silver argues gut instinct should get little weight in election forecasting because elections are rare events. Gut feelings usually amount to expecting the same thing as last time, and that reasoning is circular, as with Georgia's skeptics before 2020.
findings.evidence_quote: But in elections, I don’t think one’s gut instinct should usually be given much weight.

findings.statement: Before 2022, FLIPR's predecessors used only fancy fundamentals without the simple-fundamentals hedge, so candidate scandals like Paxton's would have carried more weight.
findings.evidence_quote: Prior to 2022, we didn’t use the “simple fundamentals” hedge, so Paxton’s scandals would have gotten more weight in the model.

findings.statement: FEC fundraising data for federal races is highly organized and serves as one of the better remaining objective benchmarks; gubernatorial fundraising data is much messier.
findings.evidence_quote: Gubernatorial fundraising data is another story.

political_insights.insight: Democrats last won Texas decisively for president in 1964 and have not won a Texas governor race since 1990 or Senate race since 1988; from 1952 to 1980 Texas was a key swing state, and it has never been liberal.
political_insights.evidence: Historical results; McGovern lost Texas by 33 in 1972.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Long losing streaks are weak evidence once the environment and candidates change.

political_insights.insight: After 2018, the Texas suburbs kept swinging blue but Democratic margins among working-class Hispanics in South and West Texas collapsed; a winning Democratic map needs both.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Demographic subgroup swings drive state outcomes and correlated errors.

political_insights.insight: VP picks generally do not matter much electorally; LBJ in Texas in 1960 is an exception.

open_questions: Functional form for converting fundraising ratios into vote margin.
